pedagogy.summary: Unequal sharing means splitting a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable method is the 'find one part' routine: add the ratio numbers to get the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply each share by its number of parts. The conceptual anchor — and the thing children most often get wrong — is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = a+b), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. Bar models make the equal-parts structure visible and are the canonical representation.
bestPractices: Teach the explicit routine: total parts = sum of the ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total parts → each share = its parts × one part.
Draw the bar model FIRST (a strip cut into a+b equal segments), label the whole, find one segment, then read off each share — diagram before arithmetic.
Make the part-to-whole fractions explicit: in 2:3, one child gets 2/5 and the other 3/5; contrast sharply with the wrong 2/3 to fence the misconception.
Convert chained/multiplicative language ('twice as many', 'three times as many') into a single ratio before sharing (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6), using the smallest quantity as one part.
Check by adding the shares back to the original total — a fast self-verification pupils can run every time.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram cut into a+b equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts) as the building block
Part-to-whole fraction strip (2/5 and 3/5 of the whole for 2:3)
Ratio table linking parts to values
commonMisconceptions: Reading the ratio 2:3 as fractions 2/3 and 3/3 (or 2/3 of the total) instead of 2/5 and 3/5 — using one part as the denominator rather than the sum of parts.
Sharing equally, ignoring the ratio (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each).
Finding the value of one part but forgetting to multiply each share back (reporting the number of parts, or one-part, as the answer).
Unable to combine chained comparisons into a single ratio, so treating 'twice as many' and 'three times as many' as unrelated.

learn.summary: Unequal sharing splits a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable routine: add the ratio numbers to find the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply the value of one part by each person's number of parts to get their share. The core idea children most often get wrong is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = sum of parts), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. A bar/tape diagram cut into (a+b) equal segments makes the equal-parts structure visible and is the canonical representation.

activities.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
feedback: If a learner tries to cut 3:5 into 3 or 5 segments, point out the two children's parts together must fill the whole strip: 3 + 5 = 8 segments, so neither 3 nor 5 can be the total.
If they answer '5 and 5' after 40 ÷ 8 = 5, respond: 'That is the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' and prompt the final multiply, then the add-back check 15 + 25 = 40.

If they say the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets, have them count the segments on the bar: the denominator is the TOTAL number of parts, so it is 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly, then test the wrong rule on its own terms — if the 3-child got 3/5, by that same rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two shares would be 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 of the sweets, more than the whole, which is impossible. That is why the denominator must be the total, 8.
If they share equally (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each), return to the bar: 3:5 means one child's part is bigger, so the numbers of segments are not equal.
If they treat 'twice' and 'three times' as unrelated, make Jo one part, so Sam is 3 parts and Tom is 6; the total is 10 parts and one part = 3 (for a 30 total). Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing.
activities.rationale: The routine is procedural and benefits from a visible equal-parts structure: a bar the learner cuts and fills gives immediate feedback when the segment count or the total is wrong, and forcing the choice of 8 (not 3 or 5) segments brings the a/(a+b) idea into the open, which is where the common 'fraction of the total is a/b' error arises.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
Pupils should solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples (Year 6 ratio and proportion).
learnerActions: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
activities.intendedInsight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.

activities.title: Explain and check the shares
feedback: Correct full response: 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, shares are 15 and 25 (which sum to 40), and the 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.
If the add-back does not reach 40, a part value or a multiply was wrong — recount segments and recompute one part.

On the 3/8-vs-5 test: 2/5 is the CORRECT complement of 3/5 (3/5 + 2/5 = 1), so 'they fit the whole' does NOT excuse the 3/5 error. Apply the misconception's own rule instead — it treats the 5-child's number of parts (5) as if it were the total, giving the 5-child 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole. That contradiction shows the denominator must be the total number of parts, 8, giving 3/8 and 5/8.
For the chained problem with 30: one part = 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so Jo = 3, Sam = 9, Tom = 18 (which sum to 30).
activities.rationale: Short reasoning prompts and an add-back check let the learner verify their own work and expose whether they counted (a+b) parts or mistakenly used a or b as the total; the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open, where 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean diagnostic split.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Answer: how many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5, and where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? Say what it would tell you if they did not.

You said the fraction is 3/8 — why is 8 on the bottom and not 5? Test the wrong rule on its own terms: if the 3-part child got 3/5, then by that same rule the 5-part child would get 5/5 (all of them) — do 3/5 and 5/5 fit inside one whole?
Given 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo, 30 altogether', turn it into one ratio (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6) before sharing, and find each share.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding the shares back to the original total is a fast self-check, and articulating why the denominator is the sum of parts secures the part-to-whole fraction and the handling of chained comparisons.

activities.title: Short questions to consolidate the routine
feedback: For 'share 40 in 3:5', the shares are 15 and 25; an answer of 20 and 20 is equal sharing that ignores the ratio.

For the fraction, 3/8 is correct; 3/5 wrongly uses the other child's number of parts (5) as the denominator instead of the sum of parts. By that wrong rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two 'shares' (3/5 and 5/5) would exceed the whole — a quick sign the denominator must be the sum of parts, 8, not 5.
For a chained problem, first state the single ratio (e.g. 1:3:6) — the multipliers are related, not separate.
activities.rationale: Targeted recall questions with distractors built from the known errors (equal sharing, a/b as the whole-fraction) help check whether the routine and the part-to-whole idea are secure. Recognition-style questions assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and cut the bar, so pair them with the bar-building task.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Share 40 in the ratio 3:5 and write the two shares.
Choose what fraction of the whole the '3' child gets.
Read a chained-comparison problem and state the combined single ratio before working out the shares.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the share values from the part-to-whole fraction lets the learner spot and discard the 'equal share' and 'a/b of the total' errors.

constraints: A static labelled bar model (cut into a+b parts, with tap-to-reveal values and part-to-whole fractions) is a useful reference/scaffold, but it does not let the learner cut and check their own segmentation — the choice of how many segments is where the key misconception surfaces, so include an activity where the learner decides the segment count themselves.
Recognition/short-answer questions assess and reinforce the routine but do not elicit independent construction of the bar or the shares; use them alongside, not instead of, the building task.
Always convert chained/multiplicative language into a single ratio (using the smallest quantity as one part, and scaling up if needed so all parts are whole numbers) before sharing.

Keep the part-to-whole fraction explicit (3/8 and 5/8 for 3:5) and contrast it directly with the wrong 3/5 to fence the misconception — and when demonstrating why 3/5 is wrong, in EVERY learner prompt and feedback item apply the misconception's own rule (3/5 and 5/5) so the contradiction (exceeding the whole) is visible, rather than its correct complement (3/5 and 2/5), which wrongly looks consistent.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted that an interactive manipulable bar 'defeats' the misconception and that a dialogue or 3D representation 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources, so they have been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance (visible equal-parts structure and immediate feedback on segment count). A fixed/static bar can still teach the routine.

Arithmetic was independently checked: 3+5=8; 40÷8=5; 3×5=15; 5×5=25; 15+25=40; fractions 3/8 and 5/8 sum to 1. Chained example with 30 total: 1+3+6=10 parts, 30÷10=3, giving Jo 3, Sam 9, Tom 18 (sum 30) — all consistent.

Independent-review correction: the flawed 3/5 counterexample survived not only in feedback but in a LEARNER PROMPT in the explain-and-check activity ('where would the matching second share come from, and could the two still fit inside the whole?'), which invites the correct 2/5 complement and can reinforce the error. Because 3/5 + 2/5 = 1 fits the whole, that framing wrongly validates the misconception. Every learner-facing occurrence now applies the misconception's own rule (the 5-child gets 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole), matching the original row's description of the error (reading 2:3 as 2/3 and 3/3).
The illustration that 3/5 of 40 = 24 can still be used to show the wrong path in feedback, but it is never presented as a valid share.

probeDeeper: How many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5? Where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? What would it tell you if they didn't?
You said the fraction is 3/8 — why 8 on the bottom and not 5? (counterexample: if it were 3/5, what would the two shares add up to?)
If instead Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo with 30 in total, how would you turn that into one ratio before sharing?
assess.correctAnswer: 15 and 25. There are 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, so one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5; the 3-part child gets 3 × 5 = 15 and the 5-part child gets 5 × 5 = 25. The 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads 3:5 as the fraction 3/5 of the whole — uses one part as the denominator instead of the sum of parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 3+5 = 8 equal segments; count them. The denominator is the TOTAL parts, so it's 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly. Reteach part-to-part vs part-to-whole vocabulary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets (or works 3/5 of 40 = 24), never forming the total of 8 parts

errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: 3:5 means the second child's part is bigger — the segments are not equal in NUMBER between children. Reteach relative-size ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 40 ÷ 2 = 20 each, disregarding that 3:5 means unequal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part but forgets to multiply each share back (reports the parts count or the one-part value as the answer)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' Prompt the final multiply and the add-back check (15 + 25 = 40).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 40 ÷ 8 = 5 and answers '5 and 5', or gives '3 and 5' as the numbers of sweets

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot combine chained comparisons into a single ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make Jo one part; Sam is 3 parts, Tom is 6; total 10 parts, one part = 3. Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing. Reteach missing-value ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On 'Tom twice Sam, Sam three times Jo, 30 altogether', treats the multipliers separately and cannot state Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally, or uses 3/5 as the fraction and shares wrongly; does not form the total of 8 parts.
responseLevels.full: Sums to 8 parts, finds one part = 5, gives 15 and 25, states the fraction of the whole as 3/8, checks by adding back to 40, and transfers the method to a chained three-way comparison (1:3:6).
responseLevels.partial: Finds one part and the correct shares (15, 25) via 8 parts, but gives the whole-fraction as 3/5, or cannot combine chained 'twice/three times' language into a single ratio — the part-whole idea or transfer is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5. Work out how many each child gets. Then tell me: what fraction of ALL the sweets does the child with 3 parts get? Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands adds the parts to get 8, so their shares total 40 and the fraction is 3/8. A child treating the ratio as a part-whole fraction says 3/5 (and often shares wrongly). Watching the working shows whether they counted 8 parts or used 3 or 5 as the total — and the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open; 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean split.
